newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS--Veba, RWE, C&W now a German telecom force.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Veba, RWE, C&W now a German telecom force.

text.p: Germany's two largest utilities, RWE AG and Veba AG and British-based Cable and Wireless said on Wednesday they will join forces to create a powerful challenger to monopoly Deutsche Telekom.

The combined networks of RWE and Veba cover thousands of miles along their vast stretch of power lines and will give the new company access to virtually every major city in Germany, in many cases reaching deep into residential neighborhoods.

It will also for the first time create a telecommunications operator in competition with Deutsche Telekom that can offer from one source a broad range of services from fixed-network telephone services to mobile communications and cable television.
"Our partnership with Cable and Wireless on the German market is strengthened by the alliance with RWE," said Veba chairman Ulrich Hartmann.

In one of the most far-reaching alliances to emerge on the German telecommunications market, RWE and the Vebacom joint venture owned by Veba and C&W will merge all their German communications networks into a new company called Netco. RWE, the largest of the two utilities, will hold a majority of 51 percent of Netco, which will provide network services and infrastructure.

A second company, called Servco, will take charge of product development, provision of service and customer management. Vebacom, in which C&W holds 45 percent, will control 51 percent of Servco. Veba AG will also take a 25 percent stake in RWE's RWECOM unit.
Vebacom and RWE will control the two companies through a joint management company located in Duesseldorf.
Vebacom will contribute its stake in the E-Plus mobile phone group and its cable television activities in Servco, while RWE will contribute its operations, including RWE Systemhaus.
RWE and Veba will merge their entire communications networks in Netco.
The deal values Vebacom at 4.2 billion marks.

The new alliance creates a powerful competitor, not only for Deutsche Telekom, but also for the DBKom alliance consisting of Mannesmann AG, German railway Deutsche Bahn AG and AT&T Corp, which has been considered the strongest of the newcomers.

Mannesmann, which owns Germany's D2 mobile phone network, plans to create a national telecommunications network by laying cable along the railway tracks. The railway already operates the second largest network after Deutsche Telekom.
While it is still uncertain how the new alliance will shape up in comparison to DBKom, Mannesmann and AT&T now have serious new competition.
"The new allinace, in my view, will be the leading competitor in Europe's biggest national market," said Richard Brown, the chief executive of Cable and Wireless, in London.
"This transaction underscores the value of our investment in Germany, materially reduces our exposure to start-up losses and will favourably impact our earnings, cash and balance sheet."

Earlier on Wednesday RWE said it would pull out of talks on a partnership with Bavaria's VIAG and British Telecommunications Plc, citing differences over strategy in plans to bid for Germany's fourth mobile telephone licence, to be awarded by the German government next year.

RWE, BT and Viag last February announced plans to build a nationwide telephone network to compete with Deutsche Telekom after the opening of the German market in 1998. Industry sources said RWE and BT had fallen out in part because of a battle for control of some of the joint activities.

RWE's decision to leave the group took share dealers by surprise. Stock in RWE, Veba and C&W initially jumped on the news, while BT and Viag suffered setbacks because of the perception their position in Germany had been weakened.
A British Telecom spokesman called RWE's defection a "hiccup" in its plans for Germany.

"We're going alone (with Viag) for the fourth mobile phone licence in Germany -- but obviously we'll need some additional partners -- maybe on the infrastructure side, or maybe on the equity side (in the longer term)," the spokesman said.
But some analysts said the company's position was dented.
"The major deficiency is that they lack some national infrastructure," said Yankee Group analyst Keith Mallinson.
Viag said it would stay the course with BT.
"The telecommunications strategy of Viag and BT will continue unchanged without the entry of RWE into the alliance," Viag said in a separate news release.
